difficultyReason: Three competing historiographical positions (James, Trouillot, Dubois) with nested comparisons across methodological commitments. The author's stance is only inferable from a pattern of qualified concessions: the author grants James his revisionist achievement, treats Trouillot's silence thesis as the most penetrating diagnostic, yet quietly withholds endorsement of Trouillot's strongest form — a reservation visible only through the asymmetric reporting verbs in paragraph 4.
passage:
For most of the twentieth century, Western historians treated the Haitian Revolution — the 1791–1804 uprising that ended French colonial slavery and produced the first Black republic in the Americas — as a peripheral episode in the larger drama of the French Revolution. C.L.R. James broke decisively with that framing in 1938, arguing in The Black Jacobins that the enslaved laborers of Saint-Domingue were not passive beneficiaries of Parisian ideals but political actors whose demands reshaped metropolitan debate. James's account, written partly as an intervention in mid-century anticolonial politics, restored the revolution to the center of Atlantic history and remains the starting point for nearly all subsequent work.

But later scholars have argued that James, for all his innovations, inherited a problem he did not fully see. Michel-Rolph Trouillot, writing in the 1990s, contends that the real difficulty is not one of emphasis but of archive — that the revolution was, for its European contemporaries, literally unthinkable, and that this unthinkability produced systematic silences in the documents James necessarily drew upon. The planter correspondence, the diplomatic cables, even the abolitionist pamphlets, Trouillot argues, were structured by categories that rendered slave self-emancipation a conceptual impossibility; a historian who corrects the interpretation without interrogating the evidentiary frame merely reproduces the silence at a higher level.

Laurent Dubois, by contrast, accepts much of Trouillot's diagnosis but resists its most sweeping form. Dubois maintains that archival silences are uneven rather than uniform: revolutionary administrators in the French Caribbean left quite detailed records of their deliberations with formerly enslaved soldiers, and regimental rolls, petitions, and judicial testimony can be read — carefully, against the grain — to recover political thought that colonial observers failed to transcribe. Where Trouillot emphasizes what cannot be known, Dubois emphasizes what has not yet been read.

The disagreement is more than methodological. James, Trouillot, and Dubois all reject the older peripheral framing, but they rank the remaining tasks differently: James sought to restore a suppressed narrative; Trouillot sought to expose the epistemology that suppressed it; Dubois seeks to extend the archive by redirecting attention within it. Trouillot's position is the most searching of the three, and the one historians now most often cite — partly because it seems to offer an immunizing metacritique of any reconstruction that proceeds without it. Yet immunity has its costs. If every new source is, by stipulation, already distorted by the categories that produced it, the resources for correction grow scarce, and the field risks settling into a cycle of diagnosis rather than discovery.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Trouillot's critique of colonial archives offers a more penetrating account of the historiography of the Haitian Revolution than either James's or Dubois's, and should be adopted without the reservations Dubois proposes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although three successive scholars have reframed the historiography of the Haitian Revolution in valuable ways, the dominance of Trouillot's archival critique carries interpretive costs that its adherents have been slow to acknowledge.

choices.label: C
choices.text: James's restoration of the Haitian Revolution to the center of Atlantic history has been superseded by later scholarship that treats his account as naively narrative.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The historiography of the Haitian Revolution is best understood as a sequence of corrections in which each scholar repairs a specific blind spot left by a predecessor.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dubois's archival practice demonstrates that the silences Trouillot identified in colonial records are less severe than Trouillot supposed.

explanations.correct: The passage surveys three reframings (James, Trouillot, Dubois), grants that each is valuable, singles out Trouillot's as the most influential and searching, and then — in the final two sentences — quietly registers the cost of that dominance. B captures both the survey and the concluding qualification.
explanations.A: Overshoots the author's stance: the passage does not call for adopting Trouillot without reservation; the final paragraph is precisely a reservation.
explanations.C: The passage says James 'remains the starting point for nearly all subsequent work,' not that he has been superseded.
explanations.D: A plausible-sounding structural claim, but the author's final point is not 'each corrects a predecessor' — it is that the newest framework has immunizing costs.
explanations.E: Attributes to the author a ranking Dubois makes, not one the passage endorses; the author is careful not to claim Trouillot's thesis is empirically overstated.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward Trouillot's position can most accurately be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: unreserved endorsement of its diagnostic reach

choices.label: B
choices.text: appreciation for its analytical power combined with wariness of its self-sealing tendency

choices.label: C
choices.text: skepticism that silences in the colonial archive are as systematic as Trouillot claims

choices.label: D
choices.text: resigned acceptance of a framework the author regards as flawed but unavoidable

choices.label: E
choices.text: enthusiasm tempered by concern that Trouillot unfairly marginalizes James

explanations.correct: The author calls Trouillot's position 'the most searching of the three' (appreciation) and then warns that its immunizing metacritique may produce 'a cycle of diagnosis rather than discovery' (wariness of a self-sealing tendency). B captures both strands at the right intensity.
explanations.A: 'Unreserved' conflicts with the final paragraph's reservation.
explanations.C: The author does not dispute the empirical reach of the silences; the concern is methodological self-sealing, not factual overstatement.
explanations.D: Too negative — the author calls Trouillot's position the most searching, not merely unavoidable.
explanations.E: The passage says Trouillot builds on James, not that he marginalizes him; this is the wrong feature to target.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A founding account is presented; two successive critiques of that account are summarized; the author evaluates the relative standing of the three positions and notes a drawback of the most influential one.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A historical event is described; three scholars offer competing factual reconstructions; the author adjudicates among them in favor of the earliest.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A methodological dispute is introduced; each of three scholars proposes a different solution; the author endorses a synthesis none of them proposed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A conventional view is stated and rejected; a replacement view is defended; two minor refinements to the replacement view are considered and dismissed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A sequence of interpretive frameworks is listed in chronological order, and the author concludes that the most recent framework is empirically flawed.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces James's founding account; paragraphs 2 and 3 present Trouillot's and Dubois's critiques; paragraph 4 ranks the three and flags the cost of Trouillot's dominance. A tracks all four paragraphs accurately.
explanations.B: The scholars are not offering competing factual reconstructions of the revolution itself; they disagree about historiographical method.
explanations.C: The author does not propose a synthesis; the final paragraph registers a concern, not a fourth position.
explanations.D: Dubois's view is not 'dismissed'; the author treats it as a reasonable moderation of Trouillot.
explanations.E: The author's concern with Trouillot is methodological (self-sealing), not empirical; describing Trouillot as 'empirically flawed' misstates the critique.

questions.questionStem: It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that the author would agree with which one of the following statements about Dubois's approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It represents a return to the pre-Jamesian framing of the Haitian Revolution as peripheral to European events.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It rejects the premise that colonial archives contain systematic silences.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It preserves the critical insight of Trouillot's position while leaving more room for new historical findings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It has displaced Trouillot's framework as the dominant approach in the field.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It treats regimental rolls and judicial testimony as unmediated records of the political thought of formerly enslaved people.

explanations.correct: The author says Dubois 'accepts much of Trouillot's diagnosis but resists its most sweeping form' and reads sources 'against the grain.' Combined with the final paragraph's worry about a cycle of diagnosis, Dubois's moderated position is precisely the kind of approach that keeps room for discovery while preserving the critical insight. C is hedged in the right way.
explanations.A: Contradicts the passage — Dubois joins James and Trouillot in rejecting the peripheral framing.
explanations.B: Too strong — Dubois accepts Trouillot's diagnosis in large part; he denies only its most sweeping form.
explanations.D: The passage explicitly says historians 'now most often cite' Trouillot, not Dubois.
explanations.E: Dubois reads sources 'against the grain,' which implies mediated reading, not unmediated transcription.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to regimental rolls, petitions, and judicial testimony (third paragraph) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the specific kinds of evidence Dubois believes can still be recovered despite the silences Trouillot identifies

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide examples of the sources James relied on in The Black Jacobins

choices.label: C
choices.text: suggest that Trouillot overlooked straightforward empirical resources available in the archive

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that colonial record-keeping was more extensive than either James or Trouillot acknowledged

choices.label: E
choices.text: introduce a fourth interpretive position distinct from those of James, Trouillot, and Dubois

explanations.correct: The list is introduced as part of Dubois's argument that 'archival silences are uneven rather than uniform' and that specific source types 'can be read — carefully, against the grain' to recover political thought. Its rhetorical function is to make Dubois's moderation concrete.
explanations.B: James is not the referent of the third paragraph; the list is attached to Dubois's methodological claim.
explanations.C: The author does not endorse the view that Trouillot overlooked these sources; Dubois's point is about unevenness of silence, not Trouillot's blindness. This is a wrong-function trap: accurate content but incorrect purpose.
explanations.D: No claim is made about colonial record-keeping being more extensive than acknowledged — the claim is about uneven silence.
explanations.E: Dubois's own position uses these sources; they do not introduce a fourth view.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following scenarios most closely parallels the concern the author raises in the final paragraph about Trouillot's position?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An economist revises a model to accommodate new data, then publishes a corrected prediction the following year.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A literary critic argues that every literary judgment is shaped by unacknowledged class position — a claim that, if accepted, discredits any rival reading in advance without requiring the critic to engage its details.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A biologist discovers that a long-used laboratory technique introduces a previously unnoticed artifact into results and retracts several earlier papers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A policy analyst synthesizes two rival schools of thought into a single framework that each school partially endorses.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A geologist refuses to accept a new dating technique until multiple laboratories have independently confirmed its accuracy.

explanations.correct: The author's worry is that Trouillot's metacritique is self-sealing: any new source is 'by stipulation, already distorted,' so rivals are discredited in advance. B instantiates exactly this load-bearing feature — a claim that wins against rivals without having to engage their specifics.
explanations.A: Model revision in light of data is the opposite of the author's concern; it is responsive, not self-sealing.
explanations.C: Retraction based on discovered artifact is ordinary error-correction, not immunizing metacritique.
explanations.D: Synthesis is a cooperative move; the author's concern is about a move that forecloses engagement.
explanations.E: Demanding independent confirmation is a standard epistemic check, not a self-sealing discrediting of rivals.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following is a claim that James, Trouillot, and Dubois all share?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The colonial archive's silences are uniform across document types.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Haitian Revolution should not be treated as peripheral to the French Revolution.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Historians cannot recover the political thought of formerly enslaved soldiers from existing records.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mid-century anticolonial politics distorted earlier accounts of the revolution.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The categories used by European contemporaries rendered slave self-emancipation unthinkable.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 4 states: 'James, Trouillot, and Dubois all reject the older peripheral framing.' That is the one claim the passage explicitly attributes to all three.
explanations.A: Uniformity of silence is Trouillot's strong form; Dubois resists it. Not shared.
explanations.C: This is closer to the strongest form of Trouillot's view; Dubois explicitly resists it.
explanations.D: The passage notes James wrote partly as an intervention in mid-century anticolonial politics but does not say the other two share a view about distortion from that.
explanations.E: This is Trouillot's specific claim about unthinkability; the passage does not attribute it to James or Dubois.

difficultyReason: Three sociological accounts of the emergence of the modern accounting profession (Larson's market-closure thesis, Abbott's jurisdictional-competition thesis, and MacDonald's cultural-authority thesis), with nested comparisons across mechanisms (credentialing, inter-professional conflict, symbolic legitimacy). The author's stance is subtly skeptical of pure market-closure accounts and sympathetic to Abbott without fully endorsing him — visible only through the distribution of reporting verbs ('argues' vs. 'establishes') and the asymmetric objections noted in paragraph 3.
passage:
The modern accounting profession emerged in Britain between roughly 1850 and 1900, consolidating through a series of chartered institutes whose members could audit the books of limited-liability firms. Sociologists have offered sharply different explanations for why this consolidation succeeded when earlier attempts had not. According to Magali Sarfatti Larson, the chartered institutes were primarily engines of market closure: by binding a credential to a legally protected title, accountants converted an ordinary service into a scarce commodity and secured rents that non-chartered bookkeepers could not. Larson's account is elegant and has been widely imitated in studies of other occupations.

Andrew Abbott acknowledges the importance of credentialing but argues that market closure alone cannot explain why the accounting institutes prevailed against rival occupations also seeking professional status. On Abbott's view, professions develop within a system of jurisdictional competition — ongoing contests in which one occupation attempts to claim exclusive authority over a particular kind of work, often at the expense of neighbors. Chartered accountants, Abbott contends, won their jurisdiction not by inventing a credential but by out-competing solicitors and actuaries for the specific task of audit once corporate statutes made audit legally mandatory. Credentialing, in this telling, follows jurisdictional success rather than producing it.

A third line, associated with Keith MacDonald, allows for both mechanisms but insists they depend on a prior resource neither Larson nor Abbott fully explains: cultural authority, the tacit trust that certain kinds of numbers, produced by certain kinds of people, deserve to be treated as facts. Without this prior trust, MacDonald maintains, a credentialed monopoly would be an empty title and a jurisdictional victory a hollow one. Clients, courts, and regulators had to come to regard the chartered accountant's signature as presumptively authoritative, and this cultural shift cannot be reduced to the institute's lobbying or its jurisdictional maneuvers.

The dispute is not symmetrical. Larson's thesis, though influential, struggles to account for occupations that achieved legal credentials but failed commercially, as several nineteenth-century surveying institutes did. Abbott's jurisdictional model absorbs this anomaly comfortably, since jurisdiction must be won against rivals and sometimes is not. MacDonald's challenge is harder to dismiss in principle, but it is also harder to operationalize: it is not clear what evidence, short of the outcome it is meant to explain, would establish that cultural authority had shifted prior to the institutes' success. Until that evidentiary question is settled, MacDonald's contribution is best understood as a standing caution rather than a rival account — a reminder that credentialing and jurisdiction do not suspend themselves in a vacuum.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Three competing explanations of the rise of the modern accounting profession are available, and only MacDonald's account of cultural authority is supported by the historical record.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Market-closure, jurisdictional-competition, and cultural-authority accounts of the accounting profession each capture something real, but on present evidence the jurisdictional account is the strongest, while the cultural-authority account functions best as a caution rather than a rival.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Larson's market-closure thesis has been decisively refuted by the historical record of nineteenth-century British professions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The emergence of the modern accounting profession cannot be explained by any single sociological mechanism and requires a fully integrated framework.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Credentialing, jurisdictional competition, and cultural authority are three stages through which every professionalizing occupation must pass.

explanations.correct: The passage surveys three accounts, notes the specific weakness of Larson's thesis (surveying institutes that got credentials but failed), credits Abbott with 'absorbing' that anomaly, and characterizes MacDonald's contribution as a 'standing caution rather than a rival account.' B captures all three assessments at the right intensity.
explanations.A: The passage does not claim MacDonald alone is supported; it specifically notes MacDonald's evidentiary problem.
explanations.C: 'Decisively refuted' overstates; the passage says Larson 'struggles to account for' certain cases, not that the thesis has been refuted.
explanations.D: The passage does not call for an integrated framework; it ranks the three unequally.
explanations.E: No claim is made about a universal sequence of stages.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following best describes the author's attitude toward MacDonald's cultural-authority thesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dismissive, on the ground that the thesis is circular

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enthusiastic, because it supplies what Larson and Abbott omit

choices.label: C
choices.text: Respectful in principle but unconvinced that the thesis has yet been given independent evidential support

choices.label: D
choices.text: Indifferent, since the thesis is outside the scope of the passage's inquiry

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hostile, because the thesis cannot be reconciled with Abbott's jurisdictional model

explanations.correct: The author says MacDonald's challenge 'is harder to dismiss in principle' (respect) but that it 'is not clear what evidence, short of the outcome it is meant to explain, would establish' the claim (unconvinced about independent support). C captures both the valence and the intensity.
explanations.A: 'Dismissive' is too strong; the author says the thesis is 'harder to dismiss in principle.' The author's worry is operationalization, not circularity per se.
explanations.B: 'Enthusiastic' is overstated; the author declines to treat MacDonald as a rival account.
explanations.D: The author engages with the thesis at length — not indifferent.
explanations.E: The author does not portray MacDonald as incompatible with Abbott; MacDonald 'allows for both' mechanisms.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any sociological account of professionalization that fails to explain commercial failure as well as success is at that point inadequate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jurisdictional competition is a sufficient condition for an occupation to achieve professional status.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cultural authority plays no role in the success of professional institutes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Market-closure mechanisms are irrelevant to the study of modern professions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: MacDonald's thesis should be accepted whenever Larson's thesis fails to fit the evidence.

explanations.correct: The author's specific complaint against Larson is that the market-closure thesis 'struggles to account for' institutes that 'achieved legal credentials but failed commercially,' and explicitly credits Abbott for 'absorbing this anomaly.' The general principle underwriting that complaint is A — explaining both success and failure matters. The inference is hedged appropriately.
explanations.B: The author treats jurisdictional competition as the strongest account but never claims it is sufficient; MacDonald's caution is taken seriously.
explanations.C: Reverses the author's position: the author says MacDonald is 'harder to dismiss in principle.'
explanations.D: Too strong; the author says Larson's account has been 'widely imitated' and never claims market closure is irrelevant.
explanations.E: The author explicitly declines to treat MacDonald as a rival account; a fallback-to-MacDonald rule is not endorsed.

questions.questionStem: The reference to nineteenth-century surveying institutes in the final paragraph functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: provide an example of an occupation that succeeded through cultural authority rather than credentialing

choices.label: B
choices.text: identify a counterexample to Larson's market-closure thesis that Abbott's model accommodates but Larson's does not

choices.label: C
choices.text: illustrate the kind of evidence that would be needed to confirm MacDonald's thesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: suggest that the chartered accountants' institute modeled itself on earlier surveying institutes

choices.label: E
choices.text: show that legal credentialing was rarely granted to nineteenth-century British occupations

explanations.correct: The surveying institutes are cited as cases of 'occupations that achieved legal credentials but failed commercially' — precisely the pattern Larson's thesis struggles with and Abbott's absorbs. Their function is comparative adjudication between Larson and Abbott.
explanations.A: MacDonald is not connected to the surveying institutes in the passage.
explanations.C: The reference is used against Larson and for Abbott; it is not offered as the evidence MacDonald needs.
explanations.E: The passage implies the opposite — that legal credentialing was granted to institutes that nonetheless failed; frequency is not claimed to be low.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations is most closely analogous to the mechanism Abbott identifies as explaining the chartered accountants' success?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A guild of metalworkers petitions the legislature for a protected title, then uses that title to restrict entry into the trade.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A newly trained group of paramedics expands its scope of practice at the expense of nurses once emergency-response legislation specifies tasks only paramedics may perform, after which paramedic certification becomes mandatory.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A regional dialect becomes prestigious because speakers of that dialect come to be regarded by the broader public as cultivated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A university redesigns its curriculum to match the entry requirements of a competitive job market.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A firm buys out its competitors and then raises prices for its services.

explanations.correct: Abbott's mechanism has three load-bearing features: (1) jurisdictional competition against rival occupations, (2) a legal change that creates a specific task, and (3) credentialing that follows the jurisdictional win rather than producing it. B instantiates all three: paramedics win a task from nurses when legislation creates it, and certification becomes mandatory afterward.
explanations.A: Matches Larson's market-closure mechanism (title-then-restriction), not Abbott's (jurisdictional contest).
explanations.C: Matches MacDonald's cultural-authority mechanism, not Abbott's.
explanations.D: No inter-occupational competition; curriculum redesign lacks the jurisdictional-contest feature.
explanations.E: Ordinary monopoly consolidation — missing the inter-professional contest and the law-driven task creation.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken Larson's account of the accounting profession's consolidation as the author presents it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several occupations in nineteenth-century Britain that did not obtain legally protected titles nevertheless achieved durable commercial dominance in their fields.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The chartered accounting institutes spent large sums on parliamentary lobbying before their credentials were recognized.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most chartered accountants in 1880 came from commercial rather than aristocratic backgrounds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Corporate statutes in the 1860s increased the demand for audit services faster than the supply of chartered accountants grew.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Non-chartered bookkeepers were able to serve small firms profitably throughout the late nineteenth century.

explanations.correct: Larson's thesis claims the legal credential is the engine of commercial success. Cases in which occupations achieved durable commercial dominance without legal credentials directly undermine that claim — the credential would not be necessary for the outcome it is said to produce. A targets the exact load-bearing feature the author's critique already flags.
explanations.B: Lobbying expenditure is consistent with — indeed supports — Larson's view that legal title matters.
explanations.C: Background of entrants doesn't affect the claim that credentials produce closure.
explanations.D: Excess demand is compatible with the credential creating scarce supply — a strengthener, not a weakener.
explanations.E: Small-firm bookkeeping outside chartered territory doesn't challenge Larson's claim about the chartered audit market; it is off-target.
explanations.other_notes: The trap to avoid is 'overreach' answers (B, D) that affect neighboring claims; the stem asks specifically about Larson's account of consolidation.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Abbott's account differs from Larson's in which one of the following ways?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Abbott denies that credentialing plays any role in professionalization, whereas Larson treats credentialing as central.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Abbott treats credentialing as a consequence of a prior jurisdictional contest, whereas Larson treats it as the mechanism producing the profession's market position.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Abbott focuses on the cultural authority of numerical facts, whereas Larson focuses on rents.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Abbott restricts his account to twentieth-century occupations, whereas Larson addresses the nineteenth century.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Abbott rejects the evidentiary record on which Larson relies.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states that, on Abbott's view, 'Credentialing ... follows jurisdictional success rather than producing it,' while Larson is described in paragraph 1 as holding that binding a credential to a legally protected title is what produces the rents. B captures the ordering contrast exactly.
explanations.A: Abbott 'acknowledges the importance of credentialing'; he does not deny it plays a role.
explanations.C: Cultural authority is MacDonald's theme, not Abbott's.
explanations.D: No such temporal restriction is mentioned.
explanations.E: No evidentiary-record dispute between the two is described.
